title: If Not Higher
hookLine: the mystical path ends in ordinary kindness
carry: the mystic's climb ends in quiet kindness
last: DEPART FROM EVIL, AND DO GOOD: BOTH HALVES.

cards: Before dawn, in the days of penitential prayers before the High Holidays, the rebbe of Nemirov vanishes. His Hasidim say he goes up to heaven to plead for them. A skeptical visitor doesn't buy it.

One night he hides under the rebbe's bed to see for himself. Before light, the rebbe gets up, puts on rough peasant clothes, takes an axe and walks out of town into the woods. The visitor follows, heart pounding.
What does a mystic do in the dark, alone, with an axe?

teach.b: Mystic kindness. The story comes from the Yiddish writer I. L.
Peretz, and it's called "If Not Higher." First, the ending. The rebbe chops wood, ties it in a bundle and carries it to a broken-down hut where a sick widow lies alone.

He tells her he's a peasant selling wood, and when she says she can't pay, he says he'll trust her. He lights her stove himself, saying the penitential prayers under his breath as he works. The skeptic watches it all.
After that, whenever the Hasidim say their rebbe goes up to heaven, the visitor adds quietly: if not higher. Second, the path you've walked.
This whole block has climbed: ten lights, broken vessels and scattered sparks, cleaving to God, a ladder of song.
And here the climb comes down to a stove and a bundle of wood. The story suggests this is where the ladder was leading all along. Third, the old teaching underneath.
The sages of Pirkei Avot say the world stands on three things: Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness.
And the prophet Micah asks: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"
Fourth, why the disguise. The rebbe hides who he is so the widow keeps her dignity.

Kindness here is quiet, unseen, and costs him his sleep. No one in the town knows, except a skeptic hiding under the bed. That's the mystic's secret in this story: the highest place may be a widow's cold hut before dawn.

how: Jews practice gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness, by visiting the sick, feeding guests, helping the poor and caring for the dead; Hasidic and kabbalistic teachers count such acts as part of the spiritual path, not apart from it.

o: a mystic's quiet, hidden act of care for someone
charity given in public so others will follow
a vision of angels that heals a sick person

p: chopped wood for a sick widow
do justly, love mercy, walk humbly

s: in the story, the rebbe really went up to heaven before dawn
he went into the woods, chopped wood and lit a sick widow's stove.
Pirkei Avot names acts of loving-kindness as one of the world's foundations
Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness.
the rebbe told the widow who he was
he said he was a peasant selling wood, so she kept her dignity.

games.q: you are the rebbe, before dawn on a day of penitential prayers. where do you go?
o: to the synagogue to pray longest.
to the woods, then to a sick widow's stove.
up to heaven, as the Hasidim say.
games.why: he chops wood, carries it to her hut and lights her stove, praying under his breath. the skeptic says: if not higher.

practice: Bring to mind someone who could use a little warmth: a neighbor, a coworker, someone at home, someone alone. Ask what would actually help them, a meal, a call, a ride, carrying something heavy, rather than what would look good.
Then picture a way to do it quietly, so it keeps their dignity and doesn't need your name on it.

wordCard.voice: Mystic kindness. The teaching, told in Peretz's rebbe of Nemirov, that the mystical climb comes down to an ordinary, quiet act of care. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: acts of loving-kindness, one of the three things the world stands on in Pirkei Avot.

carryVoice: Your line: the mystic's climb ends in quiet kindness. The rebbe of Nemirov went up, if not higher, to a widow's cold stove. I'll be here tomorrow.
